questions.text: Which three broad classes appear on the balance sheet?

options.a: Sales, gross profit, and net income
options.b: Assets, liabilities, and shareholders' equity
options.c: Operating, investing, and financing activities
options.d: Revenue, expenses, and dividends

questions.text: Why are balance-sheet accounts called permanent accounts?

options.a: Their balances carry forward from one reporting period to the next
options.b: Their balances must never change
options.c: They contain no accounting estimates
options.d: They always reflect market values

questions.text: Which characteristic is fundamental to recognizing an asset in the lecture?

options.a: An intention to create cash in a later period
options.b: Control of a resource arising from a past transaction and expected future benefits
options.c: A positive advertising campaign alone
options.d: A possible future purchase unaccompanied by any past event

questions.text: Which asset is most naturally current?

options.a: Accounts receivable expected to be collected within the operating cycle
options.b: A patent with 15 years remaining
options.c: Goodwill on an acquisition
options.d: A factory building used for 20 years

questions.text: What distinguishes cash equivalents from ordinary long-term investments in the lecture?

options.a: Cash equivalents must consist entirely of ordinary shares
options.b: Cash equivalents cannot be sold
options.c: Cash equivalents always pay more interest
options.d: Cash equivalents have an original maturity of 90 days or fewer

questions.text: What is a short-term investment?

options.a: A marketable security the firm expects to sell within the coming year
options.b: The original cost of a factory
options.c: A nontransferable patent used indefinitely
options.d: A long-term goodwill balance

questions.text: Why are accounts receivable reported net of an allowance?

options.a: Sales are always recognized only upon cash collection
options.b: Accounts receivable are never assets
options.c: Some customer balances are expected to be uncollectible
options.d: All customers must pay in advance

questions.text: What does a prepaid insurance premium represent before the coverage is consumed?

options.a: A prepaid asset
options.b: Unearned revenue received
options.c: A share repurchase
options.d: Interest expense owed

questions.text: What is operating cash in the lecture's cash analysis?

options.a: All cash held by a firm regardless of business needs
options.b: Net income earned but not distributed
options.c: Cash considered necessary for normal business operations
options.d: Only cash obtained from issuing debt

questions.text: What is excess cash?

options.a: Only cash in foreign currencies
options.b: Cash required to pay ordinary suppliers
options.c: Cash pledged to meet trade payables
options.d: Cash held above the amount needed for normal operations

questions.text: What approximate operating-cash rule of thumb is offered in the slides?

options.a: Around 1% of annual sales
options.b: Exactly 10% of shareholders' equity
options.c: Around 30% of gross profit
options.d: Around 50% of current liabilities

questions.text: How is ending inventory valued conceptually?

options.a: Quantity of remaining inventory multiplied by its assigned unit cost
options.b: Total assets less fixed assets
options.c: Net income multiplied by days sales outstanding
options.d: All revenue from goods sold

questions.text: Under FIFO, which units are assumed sold first?

options.a: The newest units purchased or produced
options.b: The units with the highest profit margin
options.c: The oldest units purchased or produced
options.d: Only the units with the lowest selling price

questions.text: Under LIFO, which units are assumed sold first?

options.a: The units with the lowest physical weight
options.b: The most recently acquired units
options.c: The oldest acquired units
options.d: Only damaged units

questions.text: Which inventory cost-flow method is not permitted under IFRS?

options.a: Specific identification where appropriate
options.b: Weighted-average cost
options.c: FIFO
options.d: LIFO

questions.text: If inventory input prices rise, which result is generally associated with FIFO rather than LIFO, all else equal?

options.a: Identical ending inventory regardless of inventory flows
options.b: Lower ending inventory and lower net income
options.c: Higher ending inventory and higher net income
options.d: Higher cost of goods sold and lower net income

questions.text: Why is FIFO said to make the balance sheet more current under rising purchase costs?

options.a: It always reports inventory at selling price
options.b: Its cost of goods sold uses the newest units
options.c: It makes all inventory non-current
options.d: Its ending inventory tends to contain newer, more recently priced units

questions.text: Why might LIFO produce cost of goods sold closer to current replacement cost?

options.a: Recent inventory costs enter cost of goods sold first
options.b: It eliminates all price-change effects
options.c: Inventory is valued at future selling prices
options.d: Oldest costs always enter cost of goods sold first

questions.text: What does inventory turnover measure?

options.a: The fraction of assets financed by equity
options.b: The days needed to pay suppliers
options.c: The percentage of credit sales collected
options.d: How many times inventory is sold or cycled during a period

questions.text: Which denominator is used in the lecture's inventory turnover ratio?

options.a: Total liabilities
options.b: Gross profit
options.c: Average inventory over the period
options.d: Closing shareholders' equity

questions.text: What is the numerator of the inventory turnover ratio?

options.a: Sales revenue
options.b: Current liabilities
options.c: Cost of goods sold
options.d: Cash from financing activities

questions.text: What does days inventory outstanding (DIO) measure?

options.a: Average number of days inventory remains before sale
options.b: Days between financial statements
options.c: Average days suppliers take to receive payment
options.d: Average days customers take to pay

questions.text: How is DIO calculated from inventory turnover using the lecture's convention?

options.a: Inventory turnover divided by 365
options.b: 365 multiplied by profit margin
options.c: Sales divided by annual interest expense
options.d: 365 divided by inventory turnover

questions.text: If inventory turnover rises while other conditions are unchanged, what happens to DIO?

options.a: DIO rises in the same proportion
options.b: DIO falls
options.c: DIO cannot change
options.d: DIO becomes equal to the current ratio

questions.text: Why can a higher DIO be economically reasonable in some cases?

options.a: A shift toward slower-selling, higher-margin products may raise DIO
options.b: DIO is independent of product mix
options.c: Higher DIO always means fewer goods held
options.d: Any higher DIO proves accounting fraud

questions.text: Which production method generally helps reduce work-in-process inventory?

options.a: Extending production waiting time
options.b: Building goods solely for speculative demand
options.c: Eliminating production bottlenecks
options.d: Increasing the number of unfinished batches

questions.text: What is the role of just-in-time deliveries?

options.a: Ensuring suppliers are always paid late
options.b: Reducing inventories of raw materials and associated holding costs
options.c: Increasing warehouses without increasing sales
options.d: Converting all finished goods into intangible assets

questions.text: What is demand-pull production?

options.a: Purchasing equipment without a production plan
options.b: Manufacturing only for highly optimistic sales forecasts
options.c: Increasing finished goods irrespective of demand
options.d: Starting production in response to actual customer demand

questions.text: All else equal, what is the immediate cash effect of reducing days inventory outstanding?

options.a: More cash must be tied up in inventory
options.b: Cash is released from inventory investment
options.c: Shareholders' equity automatically falls
options.d: Accounts receivable must increase equally

questions.text: What is an accounts receivable?

options.a: A loan the firm owes a bank
options.b: The market price of a bond
options.c: An amount owed by a customer for goods or services sold on credit
options.d: An advance payment made to an employee

questions.text: What does aging analysis of accounts receivable help estimate?

options.a: The market value of goodwill
options.b: The physical useful life of factories
options.c: The average maturity of bonds
options.d: Expected credit losses or uncollectible balances

questions.text: What is accounts receivable turnover in the course?

options.a: Sales divided by average net accounts receivable
options.b: Cost of goods sold divided by inventory
options.c: Sales divided by average accounts payable
options.d: Average receivables divided by net income

questions.text: What does days sales outstanding (DSO) capture?

options.a: Average number of days required to collect credit sales
options.b: Average inventory storage period
options.c: Average time before paying suppliers
options.d: Days from borrowing to bond maturity

questions.text: How is DSO obtained from receivables turnover?

options.a: Sales multiplied by total assets
options.b: 365 divided by the current ratio
options.c: 365 divided by receivables turnover
options.d: Receivables turnover divided by 365

questions.text: If receivables increase faster than sales, what usually happens to receivables turnover?

options.a: It equals inventory turnover
options.b: It always remains constant
options.c: It increases
options.d: It decreases

questions.text: If receivables grow faster than sales, what happens to DSO, all else equal?

options.a: It falls to zero
options.b: It increases
options.c: It is always unchanged
options.d: It becomes negative

questions.text: What might an increase in DSO signal?

options.a: Automatic improvement in collection efficiency
options.b: A reduction in the credit-sales balance
options.c: More lenient credit terms or deteriorating customer credit quality
options.d: A guaranteed increase in operating cash flows

questions.text: Which is an example of property, plant, and equipment (PPE)?

options.a: A trade receivable
options.b: Goodwill from an acquisition
options.c: A customer contract acquired separately
options.d: A manufacturing facility

questions.text: What is net PPE?

options.a: Revenue minus operating expenses
options.b: Gross recognized PPE less accumulated depreciation and relevant impairments
options.c: Current assets less current liabilities
options.d: The gross original cost plus all dividends

questions.text: What does PPE turnover measure?

options.a: Credit losses per unit of sales
options.b: Dividends per share
options.c: Interest expense per unit of debt
options.d: Sales generated per unit of average PPE

questions.text: Which change would raise PPE turnover if sales were unchanged?

options.a: An increase in average inventory with unchanged PPE
options.b: An increase in average PPE carrying value
options.c: An increase in total debt
options.d: A decrease in average PPE carrying value

questions.text: Why is higher PPE turnover often considered favorable?

options.a: It necessarily means that assets are newer
options.b: It eliminates future capital expenditures
options.c: It always proves superior product quality
options.d: It indicates greater sales relative to the invested PPE base

questions.text: What does a low PPE turnover relative to peers potentially suggest?

options.a: Greater capital intensity or underutilization of assets
options.b: No capital investment in fixed assets
options.c: Faster utilization of all machines
options.d: Automatic overstatement of sales

questions.text: Under straight-line depreciation and zero residual value, what is an estimate of average PPE useful life?

options.a: Gross profit divided by total assets
options.b: Average depreciable asset cost divided by annual depreciation expense
options.c: Accumulated depreciation divided by cash
options.d: Annual sales divided by interest expense

questions.text: Why is land excluded from the depreciable-cost base in typical PPE useful-life analysis?

options.a: Land cannot be owned by firms
options.b: Land generally is not depreciated
options.c: Land is always a liability
options.d: Land is always classified as inventory

questions.text: Why is construction in progress typically excluded from the depreciable-cost base?

options.a: Construction projects are all expensed immediately
options.b: Construction in progress is always goodwill
options.c: Assets not yet ready for use generally are not being depreciated
options.d: The balance is always held at fair value

questions.text: What does PPE percent used up approximate?

options.a: Accumulated depreciation relative to depreciable asset cost
options.b: Goodwill relative to revenue
options.c: Current liabilities divided by current assets
options.d: Total cash flow relative to total assets

questions.text: What might a high percentage of PPE used up indicate for an analyst?

options.a: An aging depreciable asset base and possible future replacement needs
options.b: A higher market capitalization by definition
options.c: An inability to earn revenue in the current period
options.d: Guaranteed absence of capital expenditure

questions.text: What is an intangible asset?

options.a: A cash deposit held in a bank
options.b: A physical factory building
options.c: An identifiable non-monetary asset lacking physical substance
options.d: Any future expectation that can never be controlled

questions.text: Which is an example of an intangible asset?

options.a: A purchased patent
options.b: Raw materials inventory
options.c: A delivery van
options.d: An accounts payable balance

questions.text: How does the lecture broadly distinguish internally generated and acquired intangible assets?

options.a: Internally generated costs are often expensed; separately acquired intangibles are generally recognized as assets
options.b: Internally generated assets are always reported as goodwill
options.c: Both are always recognized at arbitrary market values
options.d: Neither can ever appear on the balance sheet

questions.text: How are finite-life intangible assets normally treated after recognition?

options.a: They are automatically written up every year
options.b: They are amortized over their useful lives
options.c: They are never subject to any expense
options.d: They are treated as inventory

questions.text: How are indefinite-life intangible assets normally treated?

options.a: They are not amortized but are subject to regular impairment testing
options.b: They are classified as current liabilities
options.c: They are expensed when shares are issued
options.d: They are amortized over exactly three years

questions.text: What is goodwill in the acquisition accounting framework?

options.a: The fair value of all inventories purchased
options.b: Residual purchase consideration not assigned to identifiable net assets acquired
options.c: The sum of all future revenues
options.d: A firm's self-created brand value recognized annually

questions.text: Why is acquired goodwill a residual rather than a separately identifiable operating asset?

options.a: It is the same as common share par value
options.b: It is always identical to the acquiree's cash
options.c: It represents benefits not individually recognized among identifiable acquired net assets
options.d: It must be purchased separately from any business combination

questions.text: What accounting treatment applies to goodwill after recognition under IFRS?

options.a: Automatic appreciation with every sales increase
options.b: No routine amortization; impairment tests at least annually
options.c: Annual straight-line amortization over five years
options.d: Recognition as a current trade receivable

questions.text: What event may require an additional impairment assessment beyond the routine annual test?

options.a: Evidence of reduced recoverable value
options.b: A routine dividend payment alone
options.c: Issuing one new share at par
options.d: A normal seasonal increase in sales

questions.text: What happens if goodwill is impaired?

options.a: Its loss is added to operating cash receipts
options.b: Its carrying amount increases automatically
options.c: Its impairment reverses the original acquisition
options.d: Its carrying amount is reduced and an impairment loss is recognized

questions.text: For long-lived PPE, when is an impairment test typically triggered?

options.a: Only after shareholders receive dividends
options.b: On every date when revenue is collected
options.c: When facts or circumstances indicate possible impairment
options.d: Whenever the company issues an ordinary invoice

questions.text: How can a prior PPE revaluation surplus affect the recognition of a subsequent impairment?

options.a: Revalued PPE cannot ever be impaired
options.b: Every impairment must increase the revaluation surplus
options.c: A loss may first reduce the related revaluation surplus before excess reaches profit or loss
options.d: The impairment may only be recorded in cash flow

questions.text: Why examine goodwill as a percentage of total assets?

options.a: To determine the bond coupon rate
options.b: To assess how material acquisition-related goodwill is to the balance sheet
options.c: To calculate gross margin exactly
options.d: To determine inventory holding days

questions.text: Why review goodwill impairment sensitivity disclosures?

options.a: They reveal a precise future share price
options.b: They replace the audit opinion
options.c: They guarantee that future impairment will never occur
options.d: They indicate how vulnerable carrying values are to changes in key valuation assumptions

questions.text: What is common-size balance-sheet analysis?

options.a: Expressing individual balance-sheet items relative to a relevant total
options.b: Subtracting net income from financing cash flow
options.c: Using only market capitalization values
options.d: Comparing only absolute sales figures

questions.text: What is trend analysis?

options.a: Comparing competitors in one fixed period only
options.b: Comparing only dividends with expenses
options.c: Converting all items to foreign currency
options.d: Comparing a firm's financial items or ratios across different periods

questions.text: What is cross-sectional analysis?

options.a: Removing all business-model differences by definition
options.b: Comparing companies at a given point or period
options.c: Calculating a bond's present value
options.d: Comparing one firm exclusively with its own past

questions.text: Why can a cross-company comparison of PPE turnover be misleading?

options.a: PPE turnover never depends on sales
options.b: All firms use the same useful lives and impairment estimates
options.c: Firms may differ in capital intensity, leasing, asset age, and business model
options.d: PPE turnover is identical in every industry

questions.text: Why might an impairment of a large intangible asset reduce profit without immediately reducing cash?

options.a: Impairment is always a financing cash inflow
options.b: The charge is paid in cash immediately by shareholders
options.c: An impairment charge is generally non-cash at recognition
options.d: Impairment creates accounts receivable

questions.text: What is a central limitation of balance-sheet intangible values when assessing innovation?

options.a: The balance sheet must report the value of every innovation
options.b: Internally developed know-how and brands may not be fully recognized
options.c: Intangible assets are always current assets
options.d: All internally developed ideas are reported at market value

questions.text: When prices are falling rather than rising, which inventory comparison deserves particular caution?

options.a: LIFO suddenly becomes permitted under IFRS
options.b: The usual FIFO-versus-LIFO income ranking can reverse
options.c: FIFO and LIFO become identical by law
options.d: Inventory turnover can no longer be calculated

questions.text: Why is accounting for inventory relevant to comparisons of net profit margins?

options.a: Inventory valuation influences only cash equivalents
options.b: Inventory costing methods must always yield the same net income
options.c: Cost-flow assumptions can affect both cost of goods sold and reported earnings
options.d: Inventory is never recognized in the income statement

questions.text: A retailer's inventory turnover increases from 5 to 10 with unchanged selling prices and product quality. Which interpretation is most consistent with the lecture?

options.a: The retailer necessarily reports higher goodwill
options.b: The retailer's DIO doubles
options.c: Its cash conversion cycle must rise regardless of receivables and payables
options.d: The retailer holds inventory for fewer days on average

questions.text: A firm uses FIFO in an inflationary environment. Which comparison to a hypothetical LIFO firm using identical physical inventory flows is most reasonable?

options.a: LIFO is the only inventory method permitted under IFRS
options.b: FIFO reports a lower cost of goods sold and a higher closing inventory balance
options.c: FIFO reports a higher cost of goods sold and a lower closing inventory balance
options.d: FIFO and LIFO always produce identical cost of goods sold under inflation

questions.text: A firm extends its customers' payment terms from 30 to 60 days without increasing sales. Which outcome is most plausible?

options.a: DSO decreases because customers have more time to pay
options.b: Receivable turnover rises automatically
options.c: Inventory turnover necessarily falls by exactly half
options.d: Receivables and DSO increase, potentially tying up more cash

questions.text: Two firms report identical sales, but Firm A owns its factories while Firm B outsources manufacturing. What is the best caution when comparing PPE turnover?

options.a: A higher PPE turnover proves a longer useful life for assets
options.b: Both firms must report identical PPE turnover
options.c: Different operating models can explain differing turnover rates without proving different managerial quality
options.d: The firm with lower PPE must always have lower profit

questions.text: A company acquires a business for more than the fair value of identifiable net assets acquired. How is the residual normally accounted for?

options.a: Recognized as goodwill subject to impairment testing
options.b: Recognized as annual research expense
options.c: Recognized as an inventory write-down
options.d: Recognized as immediate revenue

questions.text: A firm has high accumulated depreciation relative to depreciable cost, but recently invested in new technology. Which interpretation is safest?

options.a: The ratio is unrelated to useful lives and accounting estimates
options.b: The percent-used-up ratio needs context on asset mix and recent capital expenditures
options.c: The entire asset base is necessarily obsolete
options.d: The firm's replacement capital expenditure must be zero

questions.text: A company records a large non-cash impairment loss on goodwill. Which immediate interpretation is appropriate?

options.a: The impairment represents a cash dividend to shareholders
options.b: Cash from operations must decrease by exactly the impairment amount
options.c: The firm automatically raises new equity
options.d: Accounting earnings and net assets fall, but the loss is not itself a same-period operating cash payment
